messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Fadi's Vigilance

Fadi Mansour had been a social media manager for a mid-sized tech company for eight years before the night that unmade him. At fifty-six, he had built a careful life—a marriage of thirty-one years to Layla, two adult children, a modest house in the suburbs of Columbus, a routine that suited him. He monitored brand accounts, crafted posts, managed community engagement. The work was predictable, contained. He liked predictability.

On a March evening in 2022, Fadi had been driving home from a client dinner when he was pulled over for a broken taillight he had not noticed. The officer who approached his window was young, muscular, and immediately aggressive. Fadi, a cautious man by nature, kept his hands visible on the steering wheel. He answered questions politely. He explained that he had not realized the light was broken. The officer demanded he step out of the vehicle. When Fadi complied slowly—he was thinking of his own safety, of not startling anyone—the officer interpreted the slowness as resistance. What followed was a blur of force. Fadi was thrown against the hood of his car, his face pressed into the warm metal. He tasted blood and the metallic tang of the hood's paint. His arm was wrenched behind his back, and he heard himself cry out. The officer's knee was against his spine. Fadi kept thinking: *I have done nothing wrong. I am cooperating. Why is this happening?* By the time backup arrived and the situation de-escalated, Fadi had been handcuffed, his cheek split open, his shoulder badly bruised. The charges were dropped within hours. The violation remained.

In the weeks after, Fadi found that certain sensations would trigger a flooding return of the event. The taste of iron in his mouth—whether from biting his cheek while eating or from blood work at his doctor's office—would transport him instantly back to that hood, to the helplessness, to the rage. When the memory returned, it came with an intensity of anger that frightened him. He would feel his fists clench, his jaw tighten, and he would be furious at the officer, at the system, at himself for having been vulnerable. But the memory never came through whole. He would find himself pushing it away before he could fully process what had happened, as if his mind was protecting him from something even worse than the rage itself.

Fadi began to scan his environment constantly. In his office, he positioned his desk so he could see the door. When he went to restaurants with Layla, he needed to sit facing the entrance. Before he could settle anywhere—a waiting room, a conference room, even their own living room—he would mentally map exits. His wife noticed that he had stopped watching the news, that he scrolled past videos and articles about police incidents, that he no longer watched the television shows they had once enjoyed together. She asked if he was all right. He told her he was fine, that he was just tired, but the truth was more complicated. Anything that could stir feeling—whether the news, a film, even a conversation with a friend—felt dangerous to him. He had come to believe that if he allowed himself to feel anything deeply, the rage would consume him, or the fear would paralyze him. It was safer to feel nothing at all.

At work, his distraction became noticeable. He missed deadlines. He made errors in posts that required correction. His manager asked if there was a personal issue. Fadi said no. He could not articulate what had happened to him because articulating it meant acknowledging that the world was not what he had believed it to be—that someone in authority could hurt him without cause, that the social contract he had lived by was an illusion. People were not what they seemed. The officer had seemed like someone doing a job; instead, he was someone who had violated Fadi's body and his sense of safety in one brutal moment. Fadi had acted in a way that went against everything he believed about himself—he had cried out, he had been afraid, he had been helpless. That man on the hood of the car was not the Fadi he knew.

Now, six months later, Fadi sits in the waiting room of a therapist's office, scanning the exits, unable to relax even though he knows intellectually that he is safe. His wife had insisted he come. She had said, quietly, that she could not reach him anymore, that he was disappearing. Fadi is afraid that if he begins to speak about what happened, the rage will spill out and he will lose control of it entirely. But he is also afraid that if he continues as he is—vigilant, numb, trapped—he will lose everything that matters to him. He does not know which fear is larger.
